query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating CALPHAD thermodynamic modeling with targeted differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurements enables accurate and efficient determination of the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid‐phase thermodynamic properties across high‐entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) with complex, near-equiatomic compositions.
generation.intervention: Application of a combined computational-experimental approach wherein CALPHAD modeling is used to predict fusion-related thermodynamic properties and targeted DSC measurements are performed to calibrate and validate these predictions.
generation.conditions: The approach is applied over a temperature range from room temperature up to and beyond the solidus, covering the melting transition of HEAs; it assumes availability of reliable thermodynamic data (especially from assessed binary and ternary subsystems) for the alloys of interest.
generation.structural_mediator: The solid-to-liquid phase transition and the associated configurational entropy effects that are characteristic of high-entropy alloy systems.
generation.mechanism: CALPHAD modeling captures the contributions from enthalpic and entropic terms (including configurational effects), providing quantitative predictions of fusion-related parameters; DSC experiments then validate these predictions by precisely measuring heat capacity jumps, latent heat, and volume changes at melting. The targeted DSC calibration helps fine-tune the model, compensating for database limitations and ensuring that the computed phase equilibria and transformation properties match experimental observations.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated method is expected to predict fusion properties with an accuracy within approximately 5–10% of values obtained from high-resolution DSC measurements, thereby representing an improvement over traditional single-method approaches.
generation.baseline: Traditional experimental determination of these thermodynamic properties in HEAs often relies on extensive trial-and-error paired with empirical fitting, while standalone CALPHAD predictions without targeted validation suffer from uncertainties due to limited data on complex multicomponent systems.
generation.boundary: Applicability is expected to be robust for HEAs where sufficient thermodynamic data on relevant binary and ternary subsystems exist. The approach may be less reliable for compositions or systems where database information is sparse or where unanticipated phase transformations occur beyond the modeled regimes.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in the quantitative error margin and overall predictive performance for compositions with very limited input data. The integrated method’s success depends crucially on the quality of the thermodynamic databases used and may require further refinement for HEAs with highly unconventional alloying elements or extreme melting behaviors.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a diverse set of HEA compositions across the high-entropy alloy family, including compositions at the boundaries of available thermodynamic data. Use CALPHAD modeling to predict their melting temperatures, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting. Then, perform precise DSC measurements (and complementary dilatometric studies for volume change) under controlled conditions to independently determine these fusion properties.
measurements: DSC to obtain melting onset, peak temperature, and latent heat
Dilatometry to measure volume changes at the melting transition
Comparative analysis of computed thermodynamic parameters with experimental DSC-derived values
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If more than 50% of the tested HEA compositions show discrepancies greater than 15% between the CALPHAD-predicted fusion properties and the experimentally measured values, the integrated approach would be falsified as an efficient and accurate method for determining these properties.

cited_evidence.text: The Gibbs free energy, G=H−TS, is the established thermodynamic criterion for phase selection, where H is enthalpy, S is entropy and T is absolute temperature. The Gibbs free energies for SS phases are described by enthalpies and entropies of mixing (Hmix and Smix), and IM phases are characterized by enthalpies and entropies of formation (Hf and Sf). The Gibbs free energies for all competing phases must be estimated, and the phase (or phases) with the lowest G gives the stable microstructure for that alloy. Smix, also called configurational entropy, is easy to modeland Hmix has been estimated for wide range of atom pairs. Sf for IM compounds is generally very small, and is often estimated to be zero. Hf of IM compounds is an essential term, but is difficult to estimate—there are no general models. Hmix is sometimes used as a proxy for Hf, but the differences between these values can be very large, and at best this approach gives only a relative ranking that cannot be used to determine G. The Calphad approach is used widely in the high entropy alloys and ceramics field [,,]. Senkov et al. demonstrated [] that for high entropy alloys, Calphad computations of type and number of phases agreed well with experimental results only when more than half of binary systems were fully assessed; however, even when there are enough data on binary and ternary systems, Calphad predictions of transformation temperatures, phase compositions and fractions are challenging. Compared with metals, the databases for oxides are much more limited, especially for the temperature range addressed in this study. Nevertheless, it is instructive to compare our experimental results with Calphad predictions.

The third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure Cr and V in both the liquid and A2 phases were established. By applying these expressions, the thermodynamic properties down to 0 K and thermal vacancy near the melting point can be well described. Besides, the lattice stability of Cr and V over the whole temperature range can be guaranteed. Based on the third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure elements, the Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems were thermodynamically assessed by considering the reviewed phase equilibria and thermodynamic data with the CALPHAD approach. A strategy to estimate the Gibbs energy of Laves phase was proposed by combining the theoretically computed and experimentally measured thermodynamic properties as well as semiempirical relation. Such a method was applied to C14 and C15 Laves phases in Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems. The calculated phase diagrams and thermodynamic properties showed nice agreement with the measured ones. Significant improvements can be observed at low temperatures compared with those from the second-generation thermodynamic descriptions, indicating the high reliability of the present thermodynamic descriptions.

reading.lever: Combine CALPHAD thermodynamic modeling with targeted DSC validation to predict detailed fusion properties across the HEA family.
reading.why: This integrated approach leverages proven computational predictions from refractory systems and reliable DSC measurements, addressing current database limitations efficiently.
